Thermal satellites from an Indian startup aim to spot urban heat, crop stress and wildfires from orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AHMEDABAD, India — As climate disasters grow more frequent and severe, a young Indian space-tech startup is betting it can help the world act sooner by reading Earth's temperature from orbit in near-real time.

SatLeo Labs, based here in western India, is building what it calls a "thermometer for Earth" in space. It plans to achieve its roadmap to deliver frequent, near-real-time thermal data through Pyro, a planned constellation of 15 microsatellites that will circle the planet in low Earth orbit by early 2030, if all goes to plan. Equipped with thermal sensors and onboard artificial intelligence, the satellites will measure the heat radiating from Earth's surface at a resolution finer than 10 meters (33 feet), which is sharp enough to map heat variations down to street level, the company says.

"It's going to be that precise," SatLeo Labs co-founder Urmil Bakhai told Space.com in a recent interview.

That level of detail, he said, helps distinguish temperatures across a single city and pinpoint urban hot spots, allowing governments and policymakers to plan targeted interventions and more heat-resilient city designs.

The company is also targeting agriculture, and for good reason: Research suggests that thermal data can directly reveal water stress on crops days before leaves wilt, discolor or show other visible damage, unlike visible-light satellite imagery. Other uses the company is eyeing include spotting forest fires early, tracking industrial emissions and, on the defense side, detecting sudden temperature spikes from missile launches.

Down the road, the team also envisions hyper-local uses. Near the top of its list are live heat maps built into navigation apps that could help gig-economy workers in India. These folks, who often ride motorcycles, could use the data to pick cooler routes during heat waves, said Bakhai.

"We are in space, but we're solving problems on Earth," said Shravan Bhati, SatLeo's co-founder and CEO.

First, however, the company has to prove that its homegrown hardware works in space. On Oct. 1, SatLeo launched its first technology demonstrator, TAPAS-1, aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission. Short for "Thermal Access Platform for Analytics & Solutions," TAPAS-1 is India's first commercial thermal payload in orbit and the first of SatLeo's three planned test payloads meant to validate its technology.

Once complete, the 15-satellite Pyro fleet will scan all of the world's land surface at least twice a day, Bakhai said. Successful deployment of that fleet would make SatLeo one of just a few private thermal-imaging operators across the world, such as SatVu in the U.K. and OroraTech in Germany.

The company has raised roughly $6 million since it was founded in 2023, and it holds letters of intent worth $54 million from prospective customers, Bakhai said.

SatLeo grew out of a government project that used satellite data for farming insights. Its founders found existing thermal data, such as from the U.S. government's Landsat satellites or Earth-observing craft operated by the San Francisco company Planet Labs, too coarse for India's fragmented farmlands, Bakhai said. When field teams and drones couldn't fill the gap at scale, "we realized space is the only solution," he said.

SatLeo's orbital ambitions take shape on the ground, inside a light-blocked cleanroom at the company's headquarters here in Ahmedabad. When Space.com visited in late October, about three weeks after TAPAS-1 launched, a handful of engineers in cleanroom coats were already fine-tuning its successor, TAPAS-2.

The payload itself sat perched on a solitary, nondescript table with a thick, hole-filled steel top meant to dampen vibrations from footsteps, traffic and the like. The room's only window was covered by a thick black blind to seal out stray light, a necessity for calibrating sensors meant to track the planet's thermal pulse from a few hundred kilometers up.

Despite its small size, the payload is built to collect enormous amounts of data. How much detail a payload can capture "all depends upon the architecture of the detector," said SatLeo co-founder Ranendu Ghosh, a former scientist at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO).

The design captures two infrared bands, mid-wave and long-wave, on the same payload. The company says this lets a single design serve both civilian and defense uses: long-wave suits applications like agriculture, while the hotter signatures of fires or missile launches show up better in mid-wave.

TAPAS-1 took just six months to build, and TAPAS-2 is on a similar timeline: It's expected to be ready by February 2027, according to the team.

Access to government test facilities explains much of that speed, Bhati said. Rather than buy capital-intensive equipment, such as a thermal vacuum chamber that mimics conditions in space, the company calibrates its payloads at facilities run by IN-SPACe, the government agency that supports private space firms, and ISRO's Space Applications Centre, both in Ahmedabad.

A small group of former ISRO scientists, about eight among a staff of around 40, also mentored the younger workforce and "really made this journey a little faster for us," Bakhai said.

Ghosh, who spent more than two decades at ISRO, said the nature of a private company helps, too. "When I was in ISRO, I saw people delivering this kind of a payload," he said. "I never saw it delivered in less than a year."

He credited the SatLeo team's "zeal to deliver in time," along with fewer administrative challenges than at ISRO, which he described as an organization where "you cannot bypass the hierarchy."

The harder constraint, the founders said, is not building satellites but finding rockets to carry them to space. TAPAS-1's launch slipped from a planned February liftoff to October for lack of a ride, Bakhai said.

SpaceX is reportedly not accepting new bookings until at least 2029. In addition, Skyroot Aerospace, which in July became the first Indian company to reach orbit, is still flying development missions meant to validate its Vikram-1 rocket before it begins full-scale commercial operations.

"There is a challenge right now in terms of availability of launch vehicles," Bakhai said. Once additional Indian rockets, such as those built by Skyroot and Agnikul, are flying regularly, "things will be much easier."

SatLeo is among more than 400 space startups that have emerged in India since the government opened the sector to private participation in 2020. Driven by this new wave of private enterprise, the country's space economy — currently valued at about $9 billion — is estimated to reach $40 billion over the next decade.

Asked what advice they would give newcomers entering the growing industry, SatLeo's three co-founders offered a unified message for success: start with the problem, then decide what to build.

"If you're solving a problem," Bhati said, "then people will bet on you."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#623. Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

Are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you? To leave you emotionally battered, physically exhausted, and full of despair and hope at the same time? Then allow me to prescribe a healthy dose of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth film in the Hunger Games series.

Based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. These are the biggest Hunger Games yet, with 48 tributes instead of the standard 24. Among them is Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor to series protagonists Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark.

The question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games. We know, by virtue of the entire original trilogy, that he does. But before he was the cynical, heavy-drinking, lone wolf victor audiences met in The Hunger Games, he was an optimistic 16-year-old with a caring family, a loving relationship, and a solid community in District 12. So the real question of Sunrise on the Reaping becomes, what broke that young man down so thoroughly? The answer is, unsurprisingly, bleak as all hell. But director Francis Lawrence executes it in thrilling (if occasionally overstuffed) fashion, with a Hunger Games sequence that blows series-high Catching Fire's own games out of the water, and a dogged focus on the philosophical themes at the core of Collins' work.

This being a Hunger Games movie, there are certain key beats it needs to hit. First, tributes need to be reaped. In this case, District 12's motley crew is made up of Haymitch, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). From there, the tributes must go to the Capitol and witness its gaudy depravity for themselves. They get makeovers, train, give interviews, and eventually make their way into the Capitol's ultimate death trap.

Viewers have seen these beats before in The Hunger Games and Catching Fire. They also witnessed a deliberately scaled-back version in prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which established the Games' evolution from what was essentially a run-down cage match to a glossy propaganda spectacle.

After sending us through three very different Hunger Games, how can the franchise create a new variation on the same brutal theme? First, by making Sunrise on the Reaping a heist movie. Granted, Haymitch and his allies aren't actually trying to steal anything from the Capitol. Rather, they're trying to break the arena and send a clear message. For that, Haymitch gets roped into a scheme cooked up by former victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and his son, District 3 tribute Ampert (Percy Daggs IV). With a complex series of moving parts, Ampert and Haymitch's plan captures the essence of a dangerous heist, and Lawrence delivers the suspense to match.

Then, there's the arena. If you thought Catching Fire's clock was a sadistic marvel of game-making, not to mention a visual feast thanks to its tropical jungles and beaches, get ready for a level up. The arena for the Second Quarter Quell is a technicolor nightmare. Lush flower beds and crystal clear streams hide poisonous underbellies. Swarms of beautiful birds and butterflies will kill at a moment's notice. Even an idyllic, snow-capped mountain hides explosive horrors. Thankfully, Sunrise on the Reaping is actually colorful to match, its eye-popping hues reminding blockbuster filmmakers everywhere that yes, vibrancy is still possible!

That vibrancy in Sunrise on the Reaping extends to the broader world of Panem itself, which has taken on a distinctive '70s look. The Capitol is awash in glitzy psychedelics, a far cry from the post-war dilapidation of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. As the Games have grown more extravagant, so, too have the Capitol citizens. Take District 12 escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close, almost unrecognizable under prosthetics and an uncanny tape facelift). She is the pinnacle of excess, from her visible cosmetic work to her neon fashion. Close is chewing so much scenery she could probably devour the entire arena, but it's exactly what the role calls for: ridiculous pomp, circumstance, and venomous hatred for the Districts.

Drusilla is one of the new characters introduced in Sunrise on the Reaping. However, a big chunk of the film's supporting cast is made up of familiar figures from the original trilogy: Capitol insider Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons); master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin); former victors Beetee, Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke); stylist Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning); and of course, President Coriolanus Snow (Ralph Fiennes). Their non-stop introductions give Sunrise on the Reaping an unfortunate case of prequel-itis, even if they play key roles in the story. Their presence also means the involvement of many new Capitol characters feels muted. Billy Porter's snake-loving stylist Magno Stift gets short shrift (and even shorter screen time), while his helpers Proserpina (Iris Apatow) and Vitus (Edvin Ryding) might as well be afterthoughts.

Thankfully, the District 12 newcomers fare far better. As Haymitch's great love Lenore Dove, Whitney Peak is a radiant beam of rebellious wisdom. Elsewhere, each of the tributes buck misconceptions about them to reveal their true mettle underneath. Maysilee may seem stuck-up and aloof at first, but Grace quickly unleashes the ferocious survivor in her. Wang brings kind courage to oddsmaker Wyatt, and McCann is steely sweet as Louella.

Leading it all is Zada, who does an admirable job making Haymitch his own, all while balancing Harrelson's mannerisms from the original trilogy. Put them saying "sweetheart" side by side and tell me that's not the same character, years apart.

Sunrise on the Reaping works hard to build out this captivating new version of Panem and the Games, but once it starts really playing in that sandbox, you're in for wave after wave of brutality. It's almost impressive how, after five books and six movies, the Hunger Games franchise can still find new ways to up the emotional pain of watching children fight to death under the thumb of an authoritarian regime. You'd think we'd already hit that peak with Rue's death in the first Hunger Games, and yet!

No spoilers, but let's just say I hope Zada's contract included a bonus for each time he had to cradle the body of a dear ally and tearfully beg them to stay with him. That his performance and the film never feel stale as they go through the motions of helpless grief time and time again is a testament to how distinct each of Haymitch's relationships feel.

But while Sunrise on the Reaping is arguably the Hunger Games at its most tragic, it's also the franchise at its angriest. Every instalment in the series has critiqued the Capitol, but Sunrise on the Reaping puts a laser focus on the mundane machinery that keeps these systems of power in place. As the film opens, we see Peacekeepers and Capitol staffers performing administrative tasks for the Reaping, like putting up barricades and placards dictating where children should stand. Elsewhere, the propaganda machine chugs along, with cameramen like Plutarch always finding the perfect shot to tell the Capitol's story. (And always knowing which context to leave out to make the Capitol look its absolute best.)

Throughout, though, Sunrise on the Reaping also turns its lens on Panem's citizens, asking why they allow themselves to be ruled by such a horrific regime. Collins opens Sunrise on the Reaping with several epigraphs, including two from Scottish philosopher David Hume, the first of which details his thoughts on implicit submission. The film takes that message to heart, repeatedly questioning what leads the many not to rise up against the few that govern them. Why do District 12's citizens stand mutely by while Drusilla and Plutarch re-stage a key moment from the Reaping ceremony? Why do armed tributes not turn on the unarmed Peacekeepers who oversee them at training? Sunrise on the Reaping doesn't take a subtle approach — at one point Plutarch straight-up says "no more implicit submission" — but then again, it's also vital to see a blockbuster not sand down the novel's overt messaging.

It's also vital for a film this heavy to have hope, and almost miraculously, Sunrise on the Reaping, does. The film emphasizes the fact of its title: that for Haymitch's whole life, the sun has always risen on the Reaping. But as Lenore tells him, just because that's the way things have been for so long doesn't mean they'll be that way forever. (Their conversation remixes the novel's second epigraph from Hume.)

Anyone who's watched or read the original Hunger Games series knows that Panem will one day see a world where the sun doesn't rise on the Reaping. It'll just take a lot of work and sacrifice to get there. In Sunrise on the Reaping, we get to witness the first sparks of that eventual reunion. Knowing where Haymitch's story ends turns his tragedy into a bittersweet bridge to the future, making Sunrise on the Reaping a perfect bookend to the Hunger Games franchise as it stands. (At least, until Collins decides to return to Panem.)

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters Nov. 20.

#622. Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss

Alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have identified two brain regions that show signs of deterioration earlier than the hippocampus, the area commonly examined for evidence of the disease.

The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.

By examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus. These changes may offer important new clues about how Alzheimer's develops and how it could be detected before significant cognitive decline occurs.

"We have found that there are early changes in the brain manifesting the clinical biomarkers of atrophy as much as a decade before there are clinical symptoms," said biomedical engineer and senior author Michael Miller. "It's at least a 5-to-10-year play where your brain is changing. Imagine if we could start to treat the neurodegenerative changes at the 2, 3 or 4-year point rather than after 15 years when the changes are manifesting in memory symptoms. That's the great promise here for your loved ones who are at risk."

The findings were recently published in NeuroImage Reports and are being presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

Detecting Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss Begins

Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, but the disease does not begin when someone first experiences forgetfulness or confusion. Changes associated with Alzheimer's can accumulate in the brain for decades before noticeable symptoms emerge.

Scientists believe this long period of silent progression may provide a crucial opportunity for treatment. Interventions that begin before extensive damage occurs could potentially do more to preserve memory and other cognitive abilities. However, taking advantage of that opportunity requires reliable ways to identify the disease in its earliest stages.

One promising approach involves biomarkers, measurable biological changes that can indicate the presence or progression of a disease. In Alzheimer's research, these markers could help reveal who is developing the condition before symptoms become apparent.

"Our goal is to be able to treat individuals before the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease develop so that they may delayed or even stopped," said Marilyn Albert, co-author and director of the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.

Two Brain Regions Reveal Earlier Warning Signs

To investigate where the earliest detectable changes occur, the researchers examined hundreds of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans collected through two independent research projects: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study.

The scans followed people at different stages of Alzheimer's disease over time, including individuals without symptoms, those experiencing cognitive impairment, and patients who ultimately died from the disease.

In both groups, the researchers observed a consistent pattern. The entorhinal cortex and amygdala, which are located near the hippocampus, showed greater relative tissue loss during the early stages of Alzheimer's than the hippocampus itself.

This distinction matters because the hippocampus plays a central role in memory and has traditionally been a major focus when doctors look for Alzheimer's-related brain damage.

The two newly highlighted regions perform important functions of their own. The entorhinal cortex helps retrieve previously stored memories, while the amygdala contributes to emotional memory, including how emotional experiences are processed and remembered.

Their earlier shrinkage suggests that examining these structures together could reveal signs of Alzheimer's that might be less apparent when attention is focused primarily on the hippocampus.

Brain Shrinkage Linked to Alzheimer's Tau Protein

The researchers also found an important connection between the loss of brain tissue and tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Under normal conditions, tau helps maintain the internal structure of nerve cells. In Alzheimer's, however, tau can accumulate abnormally and form tangles that interfere with healthy brain function.

Using PET imaging and digital pathology, the scientists found that areas of gray matter shrinkage overlapped with regions showing tau-related changes. Gray matter contains large numbers of nerve cell bodies and is essential for processing information throughout the brain.

This relationship strengthens the possibility that changes in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala could serve as useful indicators of early Alzheimer's disease.

The team believes that measuring tissue loss in both regions, rather than relying primarily on changes in the hippocampus, could eventually improve predictions of who is likely to develop cognitive decline.

As brain imaging becomes more accessible and less expensive, this approach could also become increasingly practical. For people with a family history of Alzheimer's or other risk factors, researchers envision a future in which doctors might examine these regions as early as a person's 30s or 40s.

"As biomarkers and treatments become increasingly available, knowing who is going to have cognitive decline is going to be really important," said co-author Meaghan Morris, a neuropathologist who studies Alzheimer's and other dementias. "This could really play into better risk stratification for identifying who is going to have cognitive decline in the near future -- and treating people earlier and earlier to hopefully slow the course of the disease."

A Potential New Path Toward Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment

Although the findings are promising, more research is necessary before doctors can use these brain changes as a reliable diagnostic tool. The study identifies potential early biomarkers, but it does not yet establish a clinical test capable of predicting Alzheimer's years in advance.

The next step is to investigate what happens within these regions at a much smaller scale. The researchers want to understand the molecular changes surrounding abnormal tau accumulation and how those changes contribute to the progressive loss of brain tissue.

Identifying the biological processes involved could eventually reveal new targets for therapies designed to interrupt Alzheimer's before extensive damage occurs.

"Our future work is to better show the molecular neighborhoods associated with these Tau protein changes as localized by these clinical biomarkers of atrophy," Miller said. "Once we know more about the molecular neighborhoods, we can develop therapies."

The Lego Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise Bridge diorama is a wonderful bit of nostalgia and a stunning recreation of a sci-fi icon. The playset features arguably feel a little out of place, given that the audience for this set will be older fans who want to board the Starship Nostalgia. But maybe that's the whole point: Making old Trek more accessible to young 'uns.

Beautiful diorama recreating the iconic sci-fi set.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

It's not quite a five-year mission, but as Star Trek celebrated its 60th anniversary in September of this year (we may have mentioned it once or twice), I decided it was high time I finally watched the original Star Trek.

Before this year, I hadn't seen a single episode of "Star Trek: The Original Series", as it's now known. I'm a millennial; I grew up on "The Next Generation", "Deep Space Nine" and "Voyager". By comparison, the old series (TOS) always looked so… old and naff whenever I saw clips of it.

But now I have seen the original series. Over the course of 2026, I've ploughed through all 79 episodes, spread across three seasons. And you know what? It's pretty damn good. Even with the shiny 2006 remasters, you'll have to prepare yourself for some bad special effects work, but the scripts are interesting, the sci-fi concepts are out there, and the acting — especially from Shatner and Nimoy — is top-notch.

And just as I finally discovered a love for this classic sci-fi series, what should drop into my lap? Why it's the new Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge diorama set from Lego. Now I have more on my wishlist to add to the Best lego space sets.

Let's start with the Band-Aid rip: this set is $200. I know; it stings, especially when Star Trek promised us a future where money doesn't exist. But at 1701 pieces (nice, I see what you did there), it's much better value from a bricks-per-dollar perspective than the X-Files set we checked out recently.

Still, that's no small investment for a toy, even if it will make a lovely display piece when it's built.

As the name suggests, you get a full Lego-ified recreation of the bridge of the USS Enterprise (NCC-1701, no A, B, C, or D). This includes Captain Kirk's chair, the helm positions ahead of him (manned by Chekov and Sulu), and all of the surrounding computer displays where you usually find Spock, Uhura and Scotty.

There's even a viewscreen that can sit in front of the crew, displaying an adorable Klingon commander facing off against Kirk.

Board the legendary starship and meet the crew of the U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 for an amazing building experience. Recreate the iconic bridge and transporter room that served as the backdrop for epic scenes from "Star Trek: The Original Series".

Alongside the main bridge, there are a few fun extras bolted on, including a rotating transporter pad (which can make minifigures "disappear") and a working turbolift door connected to the back of the main bridge diorama. You'll have to make the swoosh sound effect yourself, though.

It's a wonderfully faithful recreation of Kirk's command center, complete with computer panels and screens, swiveling chairs and that weird scope thing that Spock was always looking into.

That said, it's a little lacking in proper Easter eggs. There are some tribbles hiding around the build, and the monitors have custom stickers showing cool Trekkie things. The weapon display racks on the back hold an array of pointy Klingon blades, Starfleet phasers, Sulu's fencing rapier and even Spock's harp, but compared to, say, the X-Files set we built recently, it feels a bit lacking in those deep-cut references.

All in all, it's a fantastic little diorama, but when it was announced, I'll admit I was a little puzzled as to who it was aimed at. "Star Trek fans, duh!" is the obvious response, but the Venn diagram crossover between "people who are nostalgic for the original series of Star Trek" and "people who want to buy $200 Lego sets" has to be pretty small, right?

Star Trek first aired way back in 1966, which means the first generation of fans are now 70 years old and upwards. Lord knows I hope I'm still building Lego sets when I'm 70, but is that a large enough crowd to make this set a success? Then again the show was repeated and syndicated throughout the 70s and 80s, which means hopefully there'll be some younger buyers, too.

The playset aspects of the set are even more puzzling. The working door, exploding monitor and spinning transporter pad are great additions to a kids' playset, but this isn't that — it's a display for nostalgic Star Trek fans. The design of the set just feels a bit confused.

But then it hit me. Maybe this isn't just for fans of the original series; maybe it's meant to create some new fans. I started watching the original Star Trek 60 years after its debut because… well, I'm the sci-fi editor for a space website, and it felt wrong that I hadn't seen it. But most people don't have that sort of professional impetus. The average person won't jump back to watch a 60-year-old TV show without a polite nudge, and this set does a great job of highlighting the charm and optimism of Star Trek's debut outing.

I don't know, maybe I'm just projecting here. Maybe Lego bought the rights to make Star Trek sets and needed something to do after they'd mined all the nostalgia they could from the excellent Enterprise D set they released in 2025. Maybe this is just a toy for big kids.

Or maybe… just maybe, it's meant to inspire the next generation of Star Trek fans to check out where the magic started.

Disclaimer: We were sent a copy of the Star Trek: U.S.S. Enterprise NCC-1701 Bridge set by Lego.

#620. Feds arrest top official of healthcare company, alleging illegal drug importation

U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian company of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.

John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the company, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.

Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations. He has not yet been taken into custody.

Besides conspiracy and smuggling, the arrest warrant said John Thomas Howard was charged with introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce and illegal drug importation. No plea has been filed.

CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation last year that revealed how the company and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. The investigation found these companies have penetrated the country's healthcare system by offering high-cost specialty drugs at more affordable prices through private and public employers. In some cases, employers are requiring their staff to use an AFP.

AFPs often obtain the medications overseas and ship them directly to patients, a practice that federal authorities have said is illegal and poses safety risks. CNBC traced the trail of drugs from abroad to the U.S. via a supply chain that the pharmaceutical companies producing the medications have not authorized.

On its website, CANARX, founded in 2002 and based in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, described its business as the first international prescription provider for the U.S. and the safest such program in the industry. The company said it sources its medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand.

But the affidavit said that the FDA's investigation found "there is probable cause to believe that (CANARX) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States …."

The affidavit does not specify which medications the agency believes were illegally imported. The criminal complaint covers the period from Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026.

The company's general counsel, Joseph Morris, told CNBC in a statement: "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court."

The company has been under FDA scrutiny for several years. In 2023, the agency seized medication being shipped by CANARX that it says was potentially misbranded and counterfeit, according to an email sent to a patient that was obtained by CNBC.

And in 2019, the FDA sent a warning letter to the company, saying it was operating "in a manner that substitutes the FDA-approved drugs prescribed by the U.S. healthcare provider with unapproved drugs." Morris, in response to that warning, argued CANARX was not misleading patients, but agreed for the company to stop importing drugs that need to be administered by a doctor.

In an interview as part of the CNBC investigation, Morris said last year that the medicines shipped to U.S. patients come from highly regulated countries. He said CANARX was operating legally.

The central question for AFPs is the legality of importing prescription drugs into the U.S. for personal use. The FDA allows Americans to import medications for individual use in some cases if the drug is not available domestically. That is the basis on which the AFPs built their models for shipping medicines directly to patients.

But an FDA spokesperson told CNBC last year that "in most circumstances, a person cannot import prescription drugs from other countries into the U.S. ... as substitutes for FDA-approved drugs."

In a separate civil lawsuit that is pending, Gilead Sciences accused CANARX and other companies of illegally importing Biktarvy, its medication to treat HIV.

In a statement to CNBC on Wednesday, a Gilead spokesperson said the company "has taken strong legal action to protect patients and the integrity of the U.S. medicines supply chain. We welcome the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk."

CANARX has not responded to the Gilead lawsuit.

— CNBC's Paige Tortorelli and Melissa Lee contributed to this report

#619. Shures new spatial audio mic was made with creators in mind

Spatial audio is having a moment in the creator-verse. Just last month, Sony introduced its ECM-AX10 spatial audio mic, and now Shure is entering the category with its USB-C MV360 and MV360+ spatial audio microphones.

"We know that more and more people — more and more creators — are kind of multidisciplinary, especially for folks who are maybe video first and then they have to worry about audio second," Steve Marek, Associate Product Manager at Shure, said in a briefing with Mashable. "So, we know that there's room for that industry to grow."

Marek said, "We really wanted to think of this as a microphone that people can grow with," and that rather than having five different audio recording tools, creators can do everything with the MV360 and have flexibility with their audio output.

The MV360 retails for $349 and is available now. The microphone kit comes with the USB-C mic, a tripod, a cold shoe mic clip, a 5/8-inch mic clip, a phone clamp, two USB-C cables, a carrying case, and a foam windscreen. The microphone also has an onboard 3.5mm headphone jack.

The MV360 features four capture modes: mono, stereo, immersive binaural, and auto tracking. The latter uses virtual microphones that steer toward the loudest sound source and is ideal for recording podcasts, interviews, or moving subjects. Regardless of capture mode, you'll get a ready-to-use two-channel audio file that requires no post-production work — though it is compatible with editing apps and devices should you want to adjust or edit.

The MV360 can be as simple or as complex as you want. If you're a skilled audio engineer, you can mix to your heart's desire. Or if you've never seen audio software in your life, you have perfectly good sound straight from the mic.

The MV360+ is not available yet, but will be the more advanced option geared toward field recordists, videographers, and VR storytellers. It'll pair with DSLR cameras, action cameras, and 360 cameras. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Shure's MOTIV app is where you can set your capture mode and edit audio that you've recorded. There are plenty of presets and adjustable settings that you can play around with, too. Slide the level adjuster to capture every minor sound for ASMR or to avoid audio spiking. You can even select where the microphone is oriented in relation to the subject — whether it's facing up, down, or on its side. There's a little diagram in the app that shows a sound heat map, so you can see exactly from which direction sound is hitting the microphone.

You can record and edit directly in the app. And one really cool feature is that you can move "virtual microphones" after you've already recorded to better boost directional sound.

I received a test unit of the MV360 microphone ahead of its launch and have had a chance to play around with it a bit. It sounds great for unboxing videos — it picks up on all the crispy sounds without sounding blown out. I tested some whispering ASMR, and I was able to boost the audio levels in the companion app before recording to really pick up on every minor sound. I will be using this as an excuse to buy a bunch of weird candy from Five Below to further test the microphone's ASMR-ability, so stay tuned for that. We'll have a full review of the MV360 coming later.

My only minor frustration with the microphone is how bulky/heavy it is. With pocket mics, like the DJI Mic Mini, there's a small receiver that you plug into your phone. The MV360 plugs directly into your phone or computer via USB-C, so it's tethered to your recording device. Clamping my phone and the mic to the tripod was just a little clunky when oriented in portrait mode. But its heft also makes sense, considering how much more advanced the audio recording is compared to small creator mics.

Also, I love that Shure includes a tripod with the MV360, but I found myself reaching for my personal tripod for most of my recordings.

Neither of those are reason enough to discredit the microphone at all — just some minor learning curves.

The MV360 is available now from Shure and third-party retailers like Amazon for $349. The MV360+ will be available in early 2027 for $449.

#618. Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. These rocks, known as polymetallic nodules, contain miniature cracks and cavities that provide shelter for creatures smaller than a millimeter.

Although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean. They create hard surfaces in an environment dominated by soft mud, while their internal spaces provide additional habitats for marine life.

Polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides. They grow at an extraordinarily slow pace, often adding only a few millimeters over a million years. Found at ocean depths ranging from 4,000 to 6,000 meters, they can remain on the seafloor for millions of years.

Researchers set out to investigate the tiny organisms living within these ancient formations and determine how important the nodules are to deep-sea biodiversity.

Dr. Tanja Stratmann, a deep-sea ecologist and one of the study's three lead authors, explains: "In our study we show that the sizes of cracks inside the nodules are large enough to provide home to animals that are smaller than a millimeter in size."

Hundreds of Tiny Animals Found Inside a Single Rock

To explore these hidden habitats, the research team collected nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a vast region of the central Pacific Ocean. They used specialized sampling equipment, including box corers that collect sections of the seafloor and remotely operated diving robots capable of working at extreme depths.

Back in the laboratory, the researchers carefully opened the nodules and extracted the tiny animals concealed within their cracks and crevices.

The results revealed an unexpectedly rich community of marine life. Across 244 nodules, the team identified 4,139 individual animals. Each nodule contained an average of 17 animals, but one particularly crowded specimen sheltered an astonishing 245 individuals.

The discovery shows that these rocks are more than simple surfaces where marine organisms can attach themselves. Their intricate internal structures create three-dimensional living spaces, allowing animals to inhabit protected areas within the nodules themselves.

Dr. Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo explains: "The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor."

Hidden Ecosystems Unlike Those on the Surrounding Seafloor

Although the nodules contained fewer animals than the surrounding muddy sediment, their contribution to deep-sea life was still substantial.

For roundworms (nematodes), the number living inside the nodules amounted to approximately 10% of the number found in the surrounding sediment. For tiny crustaceans (copepods), the figure was about 25%.

However, the most important finding was not simply how many animals the researchers discovered. It was how different the communities inside the rocks were from those living in the nearby mud.

Genetic analyses revealed that the animals inhabiting the nodules formed distinctive communities. Remarkably, these communities remained highly similar across locations separated by large distances (up to 1,000 km), even though they differed significantly from the organisms found in the surrounding seafloor sediment.

This suggests that polymetallic nodules support specialized habitats that are not easily replaced by other parts of the deep ocean. Their cracks and cavities offer living conditions that certain organisms appear to depend on.

Deep-Sea Mining Could Destroy These Ancient Habitats

The findings raise serious concerns about the potential environmental consequences of deep-sea mining.

Polymetallic nodules contain economically valuable metals, including nickel, cobalt, and copper. These resources have attracted interest in industrial mining operations that would collect the nodules directly from the ocean floor.

However, removing the rocks would also eliminate the miniature habitats they contain, along with the animals living inside them.

One example is Thurammina sp. 1, a single-celled organism found particularly frequently within the nodules. This species appears especially well adapted to the sheltered spaces inside the rocks, making it an example of the specialized life that could be threatened by their removal.

The problem is that these habitats cannot quickly recover. Because polymetallic nodules require millions of years to develop, new ones would not form within a human lifetime. Mining could therefore eliminate ecosystems that would take geological timescales to replace.

Prof. Sabine Gollner warns: "Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules. This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining."

Scientists Race to Understand What Could Be Lost

The discovery highlights an often overlooked aspect of ocean conservation. Protecting deep-sea ecosystems requires more than safeguarding large, visible animals. It also means considering the microscopic and nearly microscopic organisms that inhabit specialized environments hidden within the seafloor.

An important question remains unanswered: If deep-sea mining destroys these nodule communities, could some species disappear entirely?

Researchers still need to determine whether organisms that depend on the nodules also inhabit other parts of the ocean. If certain species are restricted to these habitats, removing the nodules could potentially contribute to their global extinction.

Understanding where these animals live and how widely they are distributed will be essential for identifying areas that need protection and evaluating the potential ecological damage caused by deep-sea mining.

To investigate further, Dr. Tanja Stratmann is currently participating in an international research expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, where scientists are continuing to study the ecosystems associated with polymetallic nodules.

This expedition and other follow-up investigations are independently funded through the JPIOcean projects MiningImpact 2 and 3.

The findings reveal that even a single rock on the deep ocean floor can support a surprisingly complex community of life. As interest in harvesting the ocean's mineral resources grows, scientists are working to understand these hidden ecosystems before habitats that took millions of years to form are permanently lost.

Materials provided by MARUM - Center for Marine Environmental Sciences, University of Bremen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth.

Researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf.

During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion.

Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter.

This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place.

Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres.

ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system.

But just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova.

Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

Regional and Shiny encounters in Pokémon GO: Finishing seven days of lessons generates a unique offer code redeemable on the Pokémon GO Web Store. That unlocks Timed Research featuring XP, Stardust, and guaranteed encounters with Pikachu, Meowth, Lucario, and regional-exclusive Chatot.

#615. Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses

Astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star that rotates every eight minutes, while its companion closely resembles our own Sun.

The discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR). Their findings reveal a previously unseen combination of stars producing radio pulses and offer new clues about the origins of some of the Milky Way's most puzzling signals.

The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another. A white dwarf is the extremely dense remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers. Its companion belongs to the same general category of stars as the Sun.

Until now, astronomers had detected similar radio pulses in systems containing white dwarfs and smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. This marks the first time such signals have been identified in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.

A Rare Star System With Mysterious Radio Pulses

The newly identified pair belongs to an unusual group of astronomical objects called long-period transients (LPTs). These objects produce radio emissions that appear and disappear over periods lasting anywhere from several minutes to hours.

Despite growing interest in these strange signals, their origins remain poorly understood. The same ICRAR research team discovered the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been identified since then.

Some of these systems contain a white dwarf alongside another star, but astronomers have struggled to determine which member of the pair is responsible for the radio emissions.

The latest discovery provides an important breakthrough. For the first time, researchers have obtained radio observations detailed enough to follow a white dwarf as it travels around its stellar companion. This allows them to pinpoint the likely location of the radio pulses much more accurately.

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," said lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney.

McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, made the discovery while working at Curtin University's ICRAR branch.

To confirm the findings and examine the white dwarf's orbital motion, the researchers analyzed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Giant Magnetic Storms Detected 5,000 Light-Years Away

The radio signals revealed more than the movement of the dead star. They also gave astronomers a surprising opportunity to investigate magnetic activity on its Sun-like companion.

According to study co-author Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, the observations exposed stellar flares associated with powerful magnetic disturbances. Similar magnetic processes on our own Sun can lead to auroras on Earth when energetic particles interact with our planet's magnetic field and atmosphere.

The team also detected evidence that the white dwarf passed behind an especially magnetically active region near its companion.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence', which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface."

A stellar prominence consists of electrically charged gas held in enormous loops by magnetic fields. These structures can extend far above a star's surface, providing clues about the powerful forces shaping its outer atmosphere.

The ability to detect such activity across thousands of light-years demonstrates how much information astronomers can extract from radio signals, even when the stars themselves are extraordinarily distant.

"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away."

Powerful Radio Telescopes Reveal a Hidden Stellar Pair

ICRAR researchers have played a leading role in identifying long-period transients, and the latest discovery relied on observations from several major astronomical facilities around the world.

The system was initially detected during a sweeping radio survey of the Milky Way conducted with the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) in Western Australia.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," said Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

After the radio telescopes narrowed down the system's location, astronomers turned to the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island. Optical observations confirmed that the radio source was associated with a G-type star, establishing the presence of a companion similar to the Sun.

The MWA, led by Curtin University, operates at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia.

The MeerKAT telescope was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa's North Cape province.

Both instruments are precursors to the next generation of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. The Australian facility, SKA-Low, and the South African facility, SKA-Mid, are being developed to provide much greater sensitivity and detail when observing the radio universe.

For astronomers studying rare stellar systems, these future capabilities could dramatically expand the number of objects they can discover and reveal much more about the processes responsible for their unusual signals.

Dr. McSweeney said, "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built."

The findings were published in Nature Astronomy in a study titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion."

#614. Xiaomi 18 Pro hands-on: Undeniably cool, incredibly powerful

What if your phone had a second display on the back?

If you've asked yourself this question, or have peered lustfully at the new foldable phones, including from Apple, you should take a look at the new Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max. The display is very cool and does bring some functionality that you otherwise just cannot have, though it's not nearly as versatile as what you get with a foldable phone.

I've spent a few days with both phones, and I can tell you, these are incredibly fast, capable, and sleek devices, albeit a little iPhone-like. The display on the back is what makes them stand out from the crowd, at least visually, but it's not something that will drastically change the way you use your phone.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series is not Xiaomi's first phone to feature a secondary display on the back; last year's Xiaomi 17 Pro had one, too. Just like the main display on the front, it hasn't changed much since last year: It's still a 2.9-inch, 596x976 pixel AMOLED display, though it is a little brighter than before. I didn't get to try the 17 Pro, though, so the display on the back is new to me.

Displays: 6.9-inch, 1,208x2,624 pixel, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness; secondary display on the back: 2.9-inch, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness

Design: Dragon Crystal Glass 3 front, aluminum frame,

Size and weight: 163.4 x 77.6 x 8.4 mm; weight: 240 grams

Rear cameras: A triple rear camera system with a 200-megapixel, f/1.7 wide camera, a 200-megapixel, f/2.4 periscope telephoto camera, and a 50-megapixel, f/2.4 ultrawide camera

Front cameras: 50-megapixel, f/2.2 selfie camera

Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.

Storage: 256GB/512GB/1TB with 12/16GB of RAM

Battery life: 7,050mAh battery with 100W charging, 50 wireless, and 27W reverse wireless charging

Special features: Under display ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, stereo audio system with 3 speakers, 24-bit/192kHz hi-res audio support

Yes, this is an extremely powerful phone, even though it isn't technically Xiaomi's flagship (that's the Ultra series, which isn't out yet this year). You get the latest Snapdragon chip, a massive camera upgrade over last year's 50-megapixel system, and a humongous battery that charges very quickly.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro, which I also received for testing but have spent less time with, has a 6.4-inch display, a smaller battery, with the rest being mostly the same.

Xiaomi flagships in the numbered series follow the same philosophy: Make a phone that's very much like an iPhone, but stuff it with extremely powerful hardware for added value. It starts with the phones' names (18 Pro and 18 Pro Max), it's visible in parts of the design, and Xiaomi's HyperOS, which has been upgraded to version 4 here, can be set up to mirror iOS in almost every way.

This is not a bad thing. The Xiaomi 18 Pro is distinctive enough with its dual display that overall iPhone-likeness doesn't feel like you're having a cheap copy. And I don't mind the HyperOS software being a dead ringer for iOS, down to the near-identical Control Center (which, you guessed it, is called the Control Center on the Xiaomi as well).

Do I need a display on the back of the phone? Not really. It's useful for photos as it can give cues to the folks you're photographing, and it can take your selfies game to the next level as you can actually take selfies with the 200-megapixel main camera system. Other than that, it just looks cool.

But you do need to see it in real life to appreciate just how cool it is. It's an excellent, super-bright, pixel-dense AMOLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate. I set it up with an ocean wave animation that looks downright beautiful when I touch it. You can have AI-based apps on there, and even use it for simple games. It's so good that I kept consciously placing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max on its face when setting it on a table, just to appreciate the crispness of that mini display on the back.

But other than the camera tricks, it's still (surprise!) preferable to use the much larger front display for most tasks. But then a couple of battery breakthroughs (including silicon-carbon battery tech which Xiaomi is using here) made it to the mass market, and now Xiaomi can place an 7,050mAh battery in the regular-sized Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.

The battery charges quickly on a fast charger and it lasts for at least two days. It's so good that I didn't have proper time to really test it as I only charged the phone twice in little under a week.

I don't think I've ever used a Xiaomi phone that was as quick and worked as smoothly as this one. Playing with animated, AI-based and fancy perspective wallpapers did not punish me in terms of speed, as the phone kept operating incredibly smoothly.

But given the versatility of this phone, it's hard to blame them. One I set the phone up as I liked, the complexity of the Settings did not bother me.

We've gotten to a point in which Xiaomi can put two 200-megapixel cameras, and a two 50-megapixel ones on a phone that's not really their camera flagship.

Do we need so many megapixels? Possibly not, as evidenced in the fact that Xiaomi 18 Pro Max takes 12.5 megapixel photos by default, and you have to manually up the resolution to either 50 or 200 megapixels.

But the high megapixel count opens up interesting possibilities, such as zooming in at 12.8x without losing quality. The telephoto camera doubles as a macro camera that can go in really close (its minimum focusing distance is 12 centimetres), with Xiaomi calling it a "telescope and microscope in one."

I haven't had enough time with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera to fully assess how good it is. From what I've seen, though, it's an incredibly versatile and powerful system that you can use to squeeze out a good photo in almost every scenario.

#612. Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the data.

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."

This article was originally published in German.

#611. MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But new research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

Researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

The findings raise important questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

"We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

The study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste

Deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

In 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an important role in carrying away waste products.

That earlier discovery led to a new question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

Previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially important.

To investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

Each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

The researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

The results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings showed that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken

The researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

When a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

To measure this response, the researchers showed volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

In many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

Participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

Once again, the older group showed a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

Using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

"Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes says. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired."

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have important implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

Earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

None of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants showed signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

The relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

In a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

While older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

"It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis says. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes."

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.
